subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 15! In this unit you will become a confident handler of data – the information we collect, organise, display and interpret to understand the world. Data is all around you. When Amina records the daily temperature in Mogadishu, when Yusuf counts how many customers visit the family shop each hour, or when Halima surveys her class about their favourite fruit, they are all working with data. Learning to make sense of that information is one of the most useful skills in all of mathematics.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Tell the difference between categorical and numerical data, and between discrete and continuous data.
Design a fair survey question and collect data using a tally chart.
Organise raw data into a frequency table.
Draw and interpret bar charts and pictograms for categorical data.
Draw and interpret line graphs for data that changes over time.
Calculate the sector angles for and interpret a pie chart.
Find the mean, median, mode and range of a set of numbers.
Organise numerical data into grouped frequency tables using class intervals, represent grouped data in a bar chart, and use a ready-reckoner graph or table to look up converted values quickly.

concepts.title: Types of Data
concepts.explanation:
Before you can choose how to collect or display information, you must know what type of data you are dealing with. Getting this right is the first decision every data handler makes, because the type of data decides which charts and which averages make sense.

Categorical data sorts things into groups or categories. The answers are usually words, not amounts. Favourite sport (football, basketball, swimming), type of pet (goat, cat, chicken), and mode of travel to the masjid (walking, car, bus) are all categorical. You cannot sensibly add or average categorical data – it makes no sense to ask for the ‘average favourite fruit’. Categorical data answers the question ‘Which type?’ or ‘Which group?’.

Numerical data is counted or measured with numbers. The number of camels a family owns, the heights of students in centimetres, and the daily temperature are all numerical. Numerical data comes in two kinds. Discrete data can only take separate, usually whole, values – you can own 3 goats or 4 goats, but never 3.5 goats. Continuous data can take any value within a range, because it is measured rather than counted – a mango might weigh 214 grams, or 214.6 grams, or anything in between, depending on how carefully you measure.
concepts.example: A common trap catches many learners here: not every number is numerical data. Think about the number on a footballer’s shirt, or the number of a bus route. These are numbers, but they are really just labels standing in for names, so they are categorical. The test is simple – ask yourself, ‘Does it make sense to add these numbers or find their average?’ Adding up shirt numbers is meaningless, so they are categorical. Adding up heights gives a sensible total, so heights are numerical. Always apply this test rather than just looking for digits.

concepts.title: Collecting Data and Frequency Tables
concepts.explanation:
Good analysis depends on good data. If your data is collected carelessly, no clever chart can rescue it. The most common way to collect data is a survey – asking people a clear question and recording their answers. The way you word the question matters enormously.

A good survey question is clear and unbiased. A biased question pushes people towards a particular answer. ‘Don’t you agree that football is the best sport?’ is a leading question – it nudges people to say yes. A fair version simply asks, ‘Which sport do you most enjoy?’ and offers balanced choices. When Khadija surveys Nuur Academy about school lunches, she must be careful not to hint at the answer she hopes to hear.

As answers come in, the neatest way to count them is a tally chart. Each time an answer appears you make a single stroke, and the fifth stroke is drawn across the previous four to make a bundle of five. Counting in fives at the end is fast and reliable. This is exactly the ‘rings of ten’ idea you met with counting, but here we bundle in fives.

Once the tallies are complete, you turn them into a frequency table. ‘Frequency’ simply means ‘how many’. Suppose Farah asks 25 classmates to name their favourite fruit and records the tallies. Her finished table might look like this:
concepts.example: Always check that the frequencies add up to the number of people surveyed – here 10 + 6 + 5 + 4 = 25, which matches. This simple check catches many counting errors before they spread into your charts. A frequency table is the starting point for almost every chart you will draw, so it is worth building carefully and neatly.

concepts.title: Bar Charts and Pictograms
concepts.explanation:
Bar charts are the most common way to display categorical data. They use rectangular bars of equal width, and the height of each bar shows the frequency of that category. Because the taller bar is easy to spot, bar charts make comparison quick: you can see at a glance which category is most and least popular.

Every good bar chart has the same parts, and you lose marks if any are missing:

A clear title saying what the chart shows.

A horizontal axis listing the categories, with a label.

A vertical axis showing frequency, with a sensible, evenly-spaced scale and a label.

Bars of equal width, drawn to the correct height, with equal gaps between them.

The scale is the part learners most often get wrong. The numbers up the vertical axis must go up in equal steps – for example 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 – and the steps must be big enough to fit your largest value but small enough to read accurately. If Farah’s largest frequency is 10, a scale going up in 2s is ideal. Choosing a good scale is a real mathematical decision, not a detail.

Reading a bar chart is the reverse process. To find the frequency of a category, run your eye from the top of its bar across to the vertical axis and read the scale. If a bar stops halfway between two marked numbers, you must use the scale to work out the in-between value. Always read the title and axis labels first so you know what the numbers mean.
concepts.example: A pictogram shows the same categorical data using pictures or symbols instead of bars. Each symbol stands for a fixed number, explained in a key, such as ‘each ☺ = 2 students’. Half a symbol then means half of that number. Pictograms are friendly and eye-catching, but the key is everything: if you ignore it and simply count the pictures, you will get the wrong answer. If 5 symbols each represent 2 students, that is 5 × 2 = 10 students, not 5.

concepts.title: Line Graphs for Change Over Time
concepts.explanation:
Line graphs are the best choice when data changes over time. The horizontal axis almost always shows time – hours, days, months or years – and the vertical axis shows the quantity being measured. Each measurement is plotted as a point, and the points are joined with straight lines. The rising and falling line lets you see trends that would be hidden in a table of numbers.

Suppose Ibrahim records the temperature in Hargeisa at midday every day for a week: Monday 18°C, Tuesday 20°C, Wednesday 22°C, Thursday 25°C, Friday 23°C, Saturday 21°C, Sunday 19°C. On a line graph he plots seven points and joins them. Straight away he can see the temperature rose to a peak on Thursday and then fell back – a shape that a plain list of numbers hides.

To read a line graph, look first for the overall trend: is the line generally going up (increasing), going down (decreasing), or staying level? Then find the highest and lowest points, and notice any sudden jumps. You can also read in between the plotted points: because the line is joined, the value halfway between Monday and Tuesday is estimated as about 19°C. This ‘reading between the points’ is one of the special powers of a line graph, and it works because time flows continuously.
concepts.example: There is one important warning. It only makes sense to join points with a line when the in-between values have real meaning – as they do for temperature, which exists at every moment. If the horizontal axis showed separate categories such as ‘favourite fruit’, joining the points would be nonsense, because there is nothing ‘between’ mango and banana. So use a line graph for continuous change over time, and a bar chart for separate categories.

concepts.title: Pie Charts and Part-to-Whole
concepts.explanation:
A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors, where each sector shows a category’s share of the whole. Pie charts are excellent when you want to show how something is divided up – how a family budget is spent, or what fraction of students chose each option. Because the whole circle represents the total, pie charts answer the question ‘what part of the total is each group?’ better than any other chart.

The key fact is that a full circle contains 360 degrees, and this 360° represents everyone in your data. To find the angle for each sector, you work out that category’s fraction of the total and multiply by 360°. The formula is:

⭐ Pie Chart Angle Formula Angle for a category = (frequency for that category ÷ total frequency) × 360 degrees. All the sector angles must add up to 360 degrees.

Let us work through a full example. In a survey of 40 students about how they travel to school, the results are: Walk 10, Bus 15, Car 8, Bicycle 7. To draw a pie chart, calculate each angle by finding the fraction of 40 and multiplying by 360°:

Walk: (10 ÷ 40) × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°

Bus: (15 ÷ 40) × 360° = 0.375 × 360° = 135°

Car: (8 ÷ 40) × 360° = 0.2 × 360° = 72°

Bicycle: (7 ÷ 40) × 360° = 0.175 × 360° = 63°

Now check your work: 90 + 135 + 72 + 63 = 360°. Because the angles total exactly 360°, you know your calculations are correct. This final check is your safety net – if your angles do not add to 360°, you have made an error somewhere and must go back. You then draw the circle, measure each angle with a protractor from the centre, colour each sector differently, and add a key and title.
concepts.example: Reading a pie chart is about proportion, not exact counts. A sector that fills half the circle represents half the total; a quarter sector represents a quarter. If you know the total number of people, you can turn any fraction back into a count. Pie charts do have limits, though: they are poor when there are many small categories, and it is hard to compare two pie charts precisely. When exact comparison matters, a bar chart is often the better tool.

concepts.title: Averages – Mean, Median and Mode
concepts.explanation:
An average is a single value that stands in for a whole set of numbers – a way of describing what is ‘typical’. There are three different averages, and a big part of Year 6 is knowing not just how to calculate each one, but which to use and why.

The mode is the value that appears most often. To find it, look for the value that is repeated the most. In the data 3, 4, 4, 4, 6, 9 the mode is 4. The mode is the only average that works for categorical data – it is how we say ‘mango was the most popular fruit’. A set can have more than one mode, or none at all if nothing repeats.

The median is the middle value once the numbers are placed in order. First sort the data from smallest to largest, then find the middle. For the ordered set 78, 79, 85, 86, 88 the median is 85, the value in the centre. If there is an even number of values, there are two middle numbers, and the median is the value halfway between them – you add them and divide by two. For 78, 79, 85, 86, 88, 90 the two middle values are 85 and 86, so the median is (85 + 86) ÷ 2 = 85.5.

The mean is what most people mean by ‘the average’. You add up all the values and then divide by how many values there are. For the test scores 85, 90, 78, 85, 92, 88, 85, 79, 91, 86, the total is 859 and there are 10 scores, so the mean is 859 ÷ 10 = 85.9. The mean uses every single value, which is both its strength and its weakness.

⭐ The Three Averages Mode = the most common value. Median = the middle value when the data is in order. Mean = the total of the values divided by the number of values.
concepts.example: So which average should you use? It depends on the data. Use the mode for categorical data, or when you want the most common choice. Use the mean when the data is fairly evenly spread and you want to take every value into account. Use the median when there are outliers – unusually high or low values that would drag the mean away from what is typical. Imagine a small neighbourhood where most families earn about 400 shillings a week but one trader earns 5000. The mean is pulled far above almost everyone, so the median describes the ‘typical’ family far more fairly. Choosing the right average is a genuine mathematical judgement, not a fixed rule.

concepts.title: Grouped Data and Ready-Reckoner Graphs
concepts.explanation: So far you have organised data where every possible value gets its own row or bar, such as counting exactly how many students scored 0, 1, 2 or 3 goals. But when numerical data covers a wide range of values, listing every single value separately would make a frequency table far too long and hard to read. Instead, we group the data into class intervals — equal-sized ranges of values — and count how many results fall into each range. For example, the ages of 30 people might be grouped into the class intervals 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, 30–39 and so on, with a tally and frequency recorded for each group rather than for every individual age. Grouped frequency tables can be shown as bar charts too, but each bar represents a whole range (class interval) instead of a single value, and the bars are usually drawn touching each other since the data being grouped is continuous or closely spaced. A ready-reckoner is a different kind of tool: it is a ready-made graph or table that lets you look up a converted value quickly, without doing the calculation yourself each time. For example, a ready-reckoner graph might let you find how many kilometres correspond to a given number of miles, or how much a certain number of items costs, just by finding your starting value on one axis, tracing across or up to the line, and reading off the matching value on the other axis or column.
concepts.example: Thirty students' running times (in seconds) are grouped into class intervals: 10-14 seconds (6 students), 15-19 seconds (14 students), 20-24 seconds (8 students), and 25-29 seconds (2 students). This grouped frequency table could be drawn as a bar chart with four bars, one for each class interval, with heights 6, 14, 8 and 2. Now use a ready-reckoner: a currency conversion graph shows that 10 units of currency A trace up to 6 units of currency B. To convert 25 units of currency A without recalculating, find 25 on the currency A axis, trace up to the line, then read across to currency B, giving an instant converted value without needing to apply the exact exchange rate calculation.

methods.title: How to find the median
steps: Write all the values in order, smallest to largest.
If there is an odd number of values, the median is the middle one.
If there is an even number, add the two middle values and divide by two.

methods.title: How to find the mean
steps: Add up every value to get the total.
Count how many values there are.
Divide the total by that count.

methods.title: How to draw a pie chart
methods.example: In a survey of 20 students about favourite lunch: Pizza 8, Rice 6, Sambusa 4, Salad 2. Find each sector angle.
steps: Find the total frequency.
For each category work out (frequency ÷ total) × 360°.
Check the angles add up to 360°.
Draw the circle, measure each sector with a protractor, then add a key and title.

methods.title: Mean, median and mode
methods.example: Find the mean, median and mode of these scores: 85, 90, 78, 85, 92, 88, 85, 79, 91, 86.
steps: Solution: Mode – the value 85 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 85.
There are 10 values, so the two middle ones are the 5th and 6th: 85 and 86.
The median is (85 + 86) ÷ 2 = 85.5.

methods.title: The range
methods.example: Find the range of these daily temperatures (°C): 22, 24, 23, 25, 21, 23, 24.
steps: Solution: The highest value is 25 and the lowest is 21.
The small range tells us the temperature was fairly steady all week.

methods.title: Compare two data sets
methods.example: Class A scores 75, 80, 85, 90, 95. Class B scores 70, 75, 85, 95, 100. Which class did better, and which was more consistent?
steps: Solution: Both classes have the same mean: Class A totals 425 ÷ 5 = 85, and Class B totals 425 ÷ 5 = 85.
So on average they performed equally.
Now the ranges: Class A is 95 − 75 = 20; Class B is 100 − 70 = 30.
Class A has the smaller range, so Class A was more consistent, even though the averages are equal.

workedExamples.title: Classify the data
workedExamples.prompt: Classify each as categorical (C), discrete (D) or continuous (Con): (a) number of siblings, (b) favourite sport, (c) height in cm, (d) a bus route number.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: (a) A whole-number count, so discrete. (b) Sorted into groups, so categorical. (c) A measurement that can take any value, so continuous. (d) A number used only as a label – you cannot average bus routes – so categorical. The test each time is: can I sensibly add or measure it?

workedExamples.title: Build a frequency table
workedExamples.prompt: The number of books read in a month by 10 students: 3, 5, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 5, 4, 3. Make a frequency table and give the total.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Count how many times each value appears. 2 appears twice, 3 appears four times, 4 appears twice, 5 appears twice. So the frequencies are: 2 → 2, 3 → 4, 4 → 2, 5 → 2. Check the total: 2 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 10, which matches the 10 students.

workedExamples.title: Find the pie chart angles
workedExamples.prompt: In a survey of 20 students about favourite lunch: Pizza 8, Rice 6, Sambusa 4, Salad 2. Find each sector angle.

workedExamples.title: Mean, median and mode
workedExamples.prompt: Find the mean, median and mode of these scores: 85, 90, 78, 85, 92, 88, 85, 79, 91, 86.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Mode – the value 85 appears three times, more than any other, so the mode is 85. Median – put them in order: 78, 79, 85, 85, 85, 86, 88, 90, 91, 92. There are 10 values, so the two middle ones are the 5th and 6th: 85 and 86. The median is (85 + 86) ÷ 2 = 85.5. Mean – the total is 859; divide by 10 to get 85.9.

workedExamples.title: The range
workedExamples.prompt: Find the range of these daily temperatures (°C): 22, 24, 23, 25, 21, 23, 24.
workedExamples.solution: Solution: The highest value is 25 and the lowest is 21. Range = 25 − 21 = 4°C. The small range tells us the temperature was fairly steady all week.

workedExamples.title: Compare two data sets
workedExamples.prompt: Class A scores 75, 80, 85, 90, 95. Class B scores 70, 75, 85, 95, 100. Which class did better, and which was more consistent?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Both classes have the same mean: Class A totals 425 ÷ 5 = 85, and Class B totals 425 ÷ 5 = 85. So on average they performed equally. Now the ranges: Class A is 95 − 75 = 20; Class B is 100 − 70 = 30. Class A has the smaller range, so Class A was more consistent, even though the averages are equal.

workedExamples.title: Read a pie chart
workedExamples.prompt: A family’s monthly budget pie chart shows Housing 40%, Food 25%, Transport 15%, Savings 10%, Other 10%. Their income is 4000 shillings. How much goes to housing, and how much more than transport?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Housing is 40% of 4000 = 0.40 × 4000 = 1600 shillings. Transport is 15% of 4000 = 0.15 × 4000 = 600 shillings. Housing minus transport = 1600 − 600 = 1000 shillings more on housing.

workedExamples.title: Spot the misleading graph
workedExamples.prompt: Two bar charts show the same data: Team A 85 points, Team B 82 points. Chart X has a scale from 0 to 100; Chart Y has a scale from 80 to 90. Which makes the gap look bigger, what is the true difference, and which is more honest?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Chart Y makes the gap look bigger, because its stretched scale starting at 80 exaggerates a small difference. The true difference is 85 − 82 = 3 points. Chart X, whose scale starts at 0, is more honest. Someone might use Chart Y to make a small lead look impressive.

activities.title: Family Survey and Bar Chart
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, a pencil, and some people to ask.
steps: Choose a clear, fair question, such as ‘What is your favourite fruit?’ Offer four choices.
Ask at least ten family members or neighbours and record each answer with a tally.
Turn your tallies into a frequency table and check the total matches how many people you asked.
Draw a neat bar chart with a title, labelled axes and an even scale. Which fruit won?
Keep your frequency table – you will reuse it in Activity 3 to build a pie chart.

activities.title: One Week of Temperatures (Line Graph)
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and a way to check the daily temperature for a week.
steps: Each day at the same time, record the temperature (from a thermometer, phone or radio).
After seven days, draw a line graph with days along the bottom and temperature up the side.
Plot each point carefully and join them with straight lines.
Describe the trend: which day was hottest, which coldest, and did the week warm up or cool down?

activities.title: Turn Your Survey into a Pie Chart
activities.materials: your frequency table from Activity 1, a protractor, a compass or round object, and coloured pencils.
steps: For each category, calculate its angle: (frequency ÷ total) × 360°.
Add all your angles together and check they reach 360° before you draw.
Draw a circle, then measure each sector with your protractor from the centre.
Colour each sector and add a key and a title. Compare it with your bar chart – which shows the winner more clearly?

activities.title: The Averages Dice Game
activities.materials: a dice (or numbers 1–6 on folded paper), and a partner if available (or your AI tutor).
steps: Each player rolls the dice five times and writes down the five numbers.
Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of your own five rolls (and your partner’s, if you have one).
Check each other’s working, or ask your AI tutor to check it if you are playing alone. The player with the higher mean wins the round.
Play five rounds. Talk about how one big roll can pull the mean up but not always the median.

activities.title: Data Detective (Investigation)
activities.materials: a newspaper, a magazine, or a chart your family has seen online.
steps: Find any chart or graph and study it carefully.
Ask the ‘detective questions’: Where does the axis start? Are the labels clear? Is anything missing?
Decide whether the chart is honest or misleading, and explain why.
Redraw it more fairly if you think it is misleading. Share what you found with your teacher.

activities.title: Household Data Collection (Family Task)
steps: As a family, choose something worth measuring for a week: cups of water drunk, minutes spent reading, or how each person travels to work or school.
Everyone records their own data honestly each day.
At the end of the week, combine the data into a frequency table and choose the best chart to show it.
Discuss one conclusion your family can draw, and one decision it might help you make.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand data best? Which chart was hardest to draw accurately, and why? What surprised you in the data you collected? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Choosing the Right Average
rules.text: So which average should you use? It depends on the data. Use the mode for categorical data, or when you want the most common choice. Use the mean when the data is fairly evenly spread and you want to take every value into account. Use the median when there are outliers – unusually high or low values that would drag the mean away from what is typical. Imagine a small neighbourhood where most families earn about 400 shillings a week but one trader earns 5000. The mean is pulled far above almost everyone, so the median describes the ‘typical’ family far more fairly. Choosing the right average is a genuine mathematical judgement, not a fixed rule.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Pie Charts and Part-to-Whole.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
A pie chart is a circle divided into sectors, where each sector shows a category’s share of the whole. Pie charts are excellent when you want to show how something is divided up – how a family budget is spent, or what fraction of students chose each option. Because the whole circle represents the total, pie charts answer the question ‘what part of the total is each group?’ better than any other chart.

The key fact is that a full circle contains 360 degrees, and this 360° represents everyone in your data. To find the angle for each sector, you work out that category’s fraction of the total and multiply by 360°. The formula is:

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Averages – Mean, Median and Mode.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
An average is a single value that stands in for a whole set of numbers – a way of describing what is ‘typical’. There are three different averages, and a big part of Year 6 is knowing not just how to calculate each one, but which to use and why.

The mode is the value that appears most often. To find it, look for the value that is repeated the most. In the data 3, 4, 4, 4, 6, 9 the mode is 4. The mode is the only average that works for categorical data – it is how we say ‘mango was the most popular fruit’. A set can have more than one mode, or none at all if nothing repeats.
